Subject: Post-call technical runbook: Dedicated capacity & autoscale follow-ups

Hi Sam / Lina —

Thanks again for the call today. Short recap and proposed next steps so we have the technical work scoped on our side:

Key requirements we captured
- Steady-state throughput target: ~120 reqs/min (avg prompt ~350 tokens, responses ~150 tokens).
- Spiky bursts up to 1.2k reqs/min for 10–20 min during peak analytic jobs.
- SLO: 95th percentile p95 latency target = 250ms token start; max response latency 2.5s for median requests.
- Must run in a dedicated pool (data isolation + reserved throughput).
- Auth: token-based service account integration with your existing OIDC provider; short-lived tokens preferred.
- Integrations: SDK-based server-side calls, structured tool-calling for retrieval ops, and embedding/reranker pipeline for search re-ranking.

Open questions for sizing & architecture
1) What fraction of requests will use embeddings + rerank (adds pre/post steps)? Approx percentage so we can size CPU/CPU->GPU offloads.
2) Do you need GPU warm pools pinned to a single model family, or are mixed-model fallbacks acceptable?
3) Do you expect long-running stream sessions (continuous stream >30s) or mostly short chat/generation calls?

Immediate next steps (owner / ETA)
- Ben: Share a lightweight capacity template and demo recording from today — attached. (attached: redwood_capacity_template.xlsx; demo-recording-20260305.mp4) — by EOD today.
- Marissa: Provide a recommended autoscaling policy (min/max nodes, scaling thresholds) and concurrency guidance for the Dedicated pool and queueing pattern — by Mon, 2026-03-08.
- Rishi: Draft a short auth integration snippet showing OIDC token exchange and recommended token TTLs — by Mon, 2026-03-08.
- Sam/Lina: Send us a short sample of your embedding dimensionality and expected queries/sec for the retriever pipeline — when you can.

We can use the spreadsheet to capture estimated token/sec and model selection (we'll propose a quantization profile if you need cost reduction). Happy to hop on a 30m sizing call next week if that helps.

Best,

Thanks Ben — useful recap. A few clarifications from our side:

- Embeddings usage: roughly 30% of requests will invoke the retriever+reranker workflow (embedding creation on ingest + online re-rank per query). Batch embedding jobs will be scheduled overnight (higher token volume), but online re-rank must be low-latency.
- Models: we prefer pinned variants of the same family for inference consistency, but can accept a smaller fallback family for scale events if it preserves output quality.
- Streaming: mostly short requests; occasional streams (video captions) that can last 20–40s.

Couple of asks before we sync on sizing:
1) Can you confirm if Redwood Dedicated supports per-tenant KV cache eviction windows (we need prefix-preserving cache during a user session)?
2) How do you recommend queuing to handle the 10x burst without blowing past latency SLOs — do you suggest aggressive queueing + prioritized lanes or pre-warmed burst nodes?

We'll attach a short export of our embedding config after this email.

— Sam

From: Marissa Cole <marissa@redwood.ai>

Subject: Re: Post-call technical runbook: Dedicated capacity & autoscale follow-ups

Hi Sam — great questions. I wanted to capture recommended patterns so you have concrete defaults to evaluate:

1) KV cache / session caching- We support prefix-based KV caching scoped to tenant IDs. Eviction policies are configurable (LRU, TTL). For session-preserving behavior during a single user flow, set TTL to session length (e.g., 60m) and use LRU for cross-session eviction. This keeps the KV cache hot for short flows and evicts older prefixes under memory pressure.

2) Autoscaling and burst handling- Recommended Dedicated pool configuration for your profile:
  - Min nodes: 2 (baseline for redundancy)
  - Target nodes: 6 (handles steady-state + moderate bursts)
  - Max nodes: 18 (covers 10x spikes; warm-up time 60–90s depending on cloud provider)
  - Scale-up policy: CPU or queued-request threshold at 60% sustained over 30s OR QPS per node > 200 triggers +1 node.
  - Scale-down policy: graceful ramp-down at <30% for 2m to avoid churn.

- Warm pools vs queueing: we recommend a hybrid approach. Maintain a small warm pool (2–4 pre-warmed burst nodes) to catch short spikes. For sustained >2min bursts, use prioritized queues:
  - Priority lanes: real-time (low latency), background (batch embeddings), and rerank (short compute but may be prioritized ahead of batch).
  - Queue behavior: allow short backpressure in background lane (e.g., 10s) while real-time lanes have tighter limits; requests exceeding soft timeouts can be returned with a retry-with-backoff suggestion.

3) Concurrency limits and batching- Concurrency per GPU: recommend starting at 8 concurrent streams for generation-style requests (short prompts) and 4 for long-context/stateful sessions with KV cache hits. Continuous batching is on by default — we group small requests to maintain GPU efficiency but enforce per-request latency SLOs with a max batch-hold of 15ms for real-time lane.

4) Embedding + reranker pipeline- For online rerank: keep embedding model pinned on a small CPU+GPU tier for fast vector creation; use a dedicated GPU node pool for heavy batch encoding. We also recommend using Redwood's cached embeddings layer for frequently-seen documents to avoid re-encoding.

5) Auth / SDK guidance (quick notes)- Token exchange: OIDC short-lived tokens (5–15m) are supported. Tokens can be scoped per-role (inference-only vs admin). SDKs include automatic refresh helpers and signed request headers (x-redwood-signature) if you prefer additional HMAC verification.

I'll put a short RFC doc together with numbers (token/sec, estimated token cost, and suggested model family) based on the spreadsheet Ben sent. If you want, we can run a small performance pilot with a pinned pool for 24–48 hours to validate p95 numbers before committing.

Cheers,
Marissa
